newsitem.title: UK: Palestine official says won't concede on Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Palestine official says won't concede on Hebron.

text.p: A senior Palestinian official said on Monday his country would not give in to Israeli pressure over the West Bank town of Hebron.
Planning Minister Nabil Shaath, who is in West Europe in search of emergency aid, called Israel's closure of Palestinian borders an attempt to constrain its economy and of collective punishment.
"Israel wants to keep that pressure on so that the Palestinians will give concessions on Hebron, which of course are impossible to make," he told reporters.
U.S. Middle East mediator Dennis Ross said earlier he intended to return to Washington after the two sides failed to reach a deal on partial Israeli withdrawal from Hebron.
Israel has accused Palestinian president Yasser Arafat of backtracking on an agreement at the last minute.
Shaath said Israel's position over Hebron was "contrary to all the agreements we've signed and to the spirit and letter of the peace agreement."
But despite the difficulties, the peace process was irreversible and once it came Palestine's economy could grow and it would be able to survive without handouts.
"We will eventually have a solution...out of this conviction we are still planning for the next five years, not just the next five months," he said.
"We don't want to live on donor contributions forever. Once the (Israeli-imposed border) closures are ended for good..then we can have a self-sustaining economy."
But for now, Israel was preventing Palestine from getting its economy on track and bringing down unemployment of around 40 percent.

There could be no guarantee of lasting peace unless Palestine has the chance of economic growth, Shaath said, adding that uncertainty over the border closures meant that much of the money from donors earmarked for infrastructure projects was just sitting in banks.

Shaath is accompanied on his tour of West European donors by senior officials from the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and the United Nations -- a first for any country on this kind of mission.
"It symbolises...the critical situation that is being faced in the West Bank and Gaza and the need for funding for the Palestinian people," said World Bank resident representative Odin Knudsen.
Palestine is after an additional $20 million -- from Britain, Italy, Switzerland and Belgium -- to help balance this year's budget. It has already collected $30 million from other donors.
It meets all its donors from November 19 in Paris where it will seek further pledges for help to build up its infrastructure.
